title: Clownish Start For Trump Puppet in Colombia
author: Michael K. Smith
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Colombian_Presidential_Candidate_Abelardo_de_la_Espriella_cropped-680x482.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/18/clownish-
start-for-trump-puppet-in-colombia/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Colombian_Presidential_Candidate_Abelardo_de_la_Espriella_cropped-680x482.jpg)

Photograph Source: Abelardo de la Espriella - CC0

If Abelardo de la Espriella's first four days are any indication of what his
entire term will be like, we are in for some very dark comedy over the next
four years. Here are eight highlights from his inauspicious beginning.

(1) On Inauguration Day a clip of him looking like a fool marching in place
and saluting during military honors went viral after it was seen to have his
own military officers looking at him with a look of bewilderment as to what on
earth he thought he was doing. Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department revealed
that Colombia will receive a $1 billion support package for its participation
in Trump's Shield of the Americas project, which uses the drug war as a
pretext to attack political enemies. A car bomb exploding the same day seemed
to highlight the renewed chaos such policies are sinking the country into.

(2) President de la Espriella showed up hours late to announce Colombia's 7.4
earthquake on August 10, smiling and blowing kisses to his supporters while
offering them a "Look at me! Look at me! How ya doin?" greeting, apparently
oblivious to the buckled roads, crashed vehicles, and collapsed buildings
devastating half the country. A Latin American mini-Trump, he has captured the
required spirit of buffoonery well.

(3) His first press conference was a video of himself talking about freedom of
expression.

(4) With the country reeling from the earthquake, he took time to re-establish
relations with Israel, broken off due to Tel Aviv's mass extermination in
Palestine, and recognize the Holy State's sovereignty over Syria's Golan
Heights. Making Colombia great again.

(5) He also recognized Morocco's colonial claim to the Western Sahara.

(6) He backed Colombia out of China's Belt and Road Initiative, which the
country had spent over a decade trying to get into. The U.S. ambassador-
designate to Colombia made the announcement, not De la Espriella.

(7) He talked up Plan Patriot 2, which aims to re-start the country's
militarized coca eradication program, though it had devastating social and
environmental consequences the first time around, and is opposed by anti-
government parties and environmental, peasant, and indigenous organizations
this time. A form of chemical and biological warfare, its goal is to clear
undesired populations off rural lands desired by transnational corporations -
de la Espriella's constituency - in favor of cattle ranching, oil extraction,
and vast plantations.

(8) With lives hanging in the balance in the early aftermath of the
earthquake, he refused international earthquake aid. _We don 't need no
stinking welfare!___

Even before being sworn in, De la Espriella met with Israeli Foreign Minister
Gideon Saar, a higher priority than doing anything to help ordinary
Colombians. He also met with Javier Milei, telling the Argentine president
that the policies he is implementing served as inspiration for his own
proposed economic policy, a strange confession given that Milei's policies
have plunged Argentina's currency to its lowest value in history and provoked
massive protests, occasioning frequent street brawls outside Congress, which
are forcibly broken up with water cannons, rubber bullets, and tear gas.

Or perhaps it's not so strange. After all, De la Espriella is only
tangentially related to Colombia. A U.S. citizen who until recently lived in
Italy, his constituents are the owners of massive private wealth, their
professional servants, and Israel fanatics. Struggling Colombians are for him
no more than a minor irritant to be quickly brushed aside, like ants at a
picnic.

His career focus has been as a lawyer for the AUC, a paramilitary conglomerate
that sowed terror and massacre in Colombia for decades, a war on the poor that
painstakingly evolved into a peace and reconciliation process in 2016, which
De la Espriella now eagerly seeks to unravel. The negotiations ended
Colombia's forty-year civil war, disarmed over 11,000 combatants, transformed
the rebel group into the Comunes political party, and established the Special
Jurisdiction for Peace to deliver transitional justice and landmark
restorative sentences for victims while reintegrating thousands of ex-
combatants into civilian life through community and cooperative projects. For
many of those who laid down their arms, however, their reward has been getting
assassinated or disappeared by death squads.

In the recent elections, outgoing Gustavo Petro and his would-be successor
Ivan Cepeda represented the path of continuing the peace process in order to
complete a social transformation that would eliminate the mass poverty and
injustice that are the driving force behind political violence, which the
right seeks to repress, not resolve. In short, the choice Colombian voters
faced at the ballot box was between striving for social peace nonviolently or
taking a giant step towards unrestrained state warfare against the common
people, a policy that cannot bring social peace short of complete
extermination. The overwhelming majority of Colombians didn't endorse De le
Espriella's iron fist agenda, either by staying home or voting for other
candidates.

Unpopular though it may be, De la Espriella honed that agenda for years as a
lawyer helping figures like Jorge Caballero, Rocio Arias, and Eleonora Pineda,
spokespersons for the paramilitary AUC in Congress who were convicted of
parapolitics, as well as Juan Carlos, "El Tuso Sierra," a former drug-
trafficker and also a member of the AUC. But his most prominent client was ex-
president Álvaro Uribe, whom he has advised regarding the judicial process
opened by former House representative for Bogotá, Iván Cepeda. Today Cepeda
says, "Paramilitarism created an apparatus of death that erected an immense
mountain of corpses upon which the pinnacle of power in Colombia was reached."
His recent presidential candidacy sought justice against the narco-
paramilitary Uribe and his most ardent defender–De la Espriella–who as a U.S.
citizen had to swear absolute loyalty to Washington, effectively an oath of
patriotic loyalty to the empire that sponsors all the political violence.

Uribe's election in 2002 inaugurated one of the bloodiest campaigns of state
terror in Colombia's history, with Colombian state and paramilitary forces
committing about 80% of the country's human rights crimes, compared to 16% by
guerrillas. The death squads were not independent of the Colombian state, as
was frequently declared by Washington, but an outgrowth of it: police even
patrolled alongside the paramilitaries.

Not surprisingly, Uribe's name turned up in the files of the U.S. DEA and the
CIA as a narcotrafficker, one of the most wanted international drug
traffickers, in fact. A declassified National Security Agency report dated
September 23, 1991 described him as a collaborator of the Medellin cartel and
a personal friend of the notorious Pablo Escobar, who former Colombian
presidential candidate and one-time FARC hostage Ingrid Betancourt described
as a "monster who had shown his fourteen-year-old son how to dig out a
victim's eyeball with a red-hot spoon." Such are the realities of iron-fist
politics in Colombia. The DEA report states that Uribe was one of the "more
important Colombian narco-terrorists contracted by the Colombian narcotics
cartels for security, transportation, distribution, collection, and
enforcement of narcotics operations in both the United States and Colombia.
These individuals were also contracted as 'hit men' to assassinate individuals
. . . . and to perform terrorist attacks against Colombian officials, other
government officials, law enforcement agencies, and groups of other political
persuasions."

A key feature of the vicious class warfare of those years was the funding of a
31,000-member-strong death squad that sowed terror throughout the country,
killing thousands of peasants wherever the FARC (Revolutionary Armed Forces of
Colombia) guerrillas were influential. Hundreds of trade union activists were
assassinated by hit men in broad daylight in towns and cities occupied by the
army. Human rights workers, as well as journalists and professors who dared to
report on military massacres, were kidnapped, tortured, and killed, some
beheaded or disemboweled.

Millions of peasants were driven off their land and herded into wretched urban
slums, the land taken over by prominent paramilitary chiefs or large
landowners. This purging of political undesirables was strictly in accordance
with Pentagon counter-insurgency training, which counseled the Colombian
military to destroy the "social infrastructure" of the FARC, including its
longstanding and extensive family, community, and social ties with the
peasantry. The goal was to annihilate the social support the guerrillas
depended on to survive, not negotiate a way for them to survive differently.
Not without reason was Colombia called "the genocidal democracy."* Virtually
all of its human rights abuses went unpunished.

Instead of addressing the savage poverty that was the root of the war, Uribe
perpetuated it while viciously attacking the inevitable guerrilla response. In
a country of 45 million people, about 11 million could not afford even one
nutritious meal a day and close to two-thirds of the population could not
afford to meet its most basic subsistence needs. In rural areas, there were
virtually no decent roads, schools, or hospitals, and the poverty rate rose as
high as 85%. Such a status quo could only be maintained by major applications
of state violence, which is to say, death squads.

A complete bill of indictment against Uribe would take considerable time to
draw up. He openly collaborated in the crimes of the death squads; caused
massive forced displacement - over four million Colombians were uprooted from
the land; ignored structural problems in the economy perpetuating massive
unemployment and under-employment; allowed funds for the poor and social
sectors to be systematically transferred to drug lords, paramilitaries, rich
industrialists, and personal friends; denationalized companies in the
telecommunications, oil, and mining sectors; closed down some of Colombia's
biggest hospitals, eliminating over four thousand medical jobs; systematically
murdered union organizers, illegally invaded Ecuador; used the judicial system
to attack civilians and political opponents; illegally assigned contracts to
personal relatives; violated Colombian sovereignty by permitting seven U.S.
military bases in Colombia (the Colombian Constitution does not allow the
stationing of foreign troops on Colombian soil). In short, he worked long and
diligently to convert the Colombian state into a major criminal enterprise.

De la Espriella differs from Uribe in depending more on personal charisma than
traditional party structures, but he clearly builds on Uribe's hardline
security legacy while only superficially breaking with the Colombian
establishment. According to Mexican journalist Sasi Alejandre, De la
Espriella, who ran for president as a political "outsider," is possibly the
most well-connected "outsider" that Colombia has ever had. He comes from a
wealthy family close to Álvaro Uribe in the department of Cordoba. In his
youth, he founded a "peace foundation," FIPAZ, which was actually funded by
the paramilitaries themselves, specifically by Salvatore Mancuso, the historic
and bloodthirsty commander of the paramilitary AUC, who promoted candidates
close to the paramilitaries, including Uribe, and dedicated the organization
to making public speeches on university campuses promoting the paramilitaries.

Espriella focuses on the "free market" and "merit," and has promised to reduce
the size of the Colombian state by up to 40% in order to provide what the late
Edward Herman called a "favorable investment climate." That's a climate where
taxes are low, profit repatriation allowances generous, poor people too
terrified to lift their heads, independent journalists dead or in jail, and
workplace and environmental regulations weak or non-existent. This is
practically a description of utopia from De la Espriella's point of view
(right-wing libertarianism), and he's eagerly pursuing the capitalist promised
land. He favors "flexible" labor (subordinate to capital) and "productive"
environmental regulation (pro-growth), and since taking office on August 7,
has announced the repeal of the wealth tax, a levy applied only to those
holding liquid assets in excess of 20 million pesos, a tiny minority of
Colombians. Meanwhile, his Finance Minister Miguel Gomez Martinez plans a
budget cut of at least 20 trillion Colombian pesos, approximately six billion
U.S. dollars, which would require a halt to almost all government spending to
implement.

In short, the DOGE plan. What could go wrong?
